title: TensorRT/Triton/Custom-kernel integration experiments and tradeoffs (draft)
content:
SUMMARY
This is a working notes doc capturing experiments integrating TensorRT (TRT) backends via Triton and a smaller custom-kernel path we prototyped for specific attention/block-sparse ops. Goal: quantify perf/latency/cost tradeoffs, understand KV cache interactions and scheduling implications, and propose a recommended integration approach for the serving runtime.

Status: draft. Most experiments run on p4d/p100-like nodes in staging. Numbers are preliminary and workload-dependent.

GOALS
- Measure token/sec and 95p latency for common LLM shapes when using: native Triton TRT runtimes, TRT with custom fused kernels, and our custom-kernel-inference path (bypassing Triton).
- Validate KV cache correctness and memory behavior across modes (shared cache, per-stream, serialized/deserialized).
- Explore scheduling/backpressure effects when mixing Triton queues + custom CUDA kernels + runtime batching.
- Surface operational complexity and maintenance cost (build/tooling, Triton compatibility matrix, debugging).

EXPERIMENT SETUP
- Models: Llama-2-13B (fp16 / q8_0 fast path), Mix: 2 fixed context lengths (512 and 2048) and two request distributions (single-turn 32 tokens, mult-turn 512 tokens).
- HW: 4x A100-40GB (emulated p4 equivalent) and 2x T4 for mixed-capacity runs.
- Runtimes tested:
  - Triton->TensorRT native conversion (canonical workflow, TRT engine per model/seq-len).
  - Triton->TensorRT with custom fused attention kernel (we added plugin layer for rotary+QKV fusion).
  - Custom runtime path: serving runtime launches our CUDA kernels directly, manual memory mgmt, batched prefix KV merging implemented in-host.
- Batching: dynamic batching window 5ms and 25ms policies. Also disabled batching for latency SLO runs.
- KV cache: two modes tested: shared KV cache (one large GPU buffer per model pinned and indexed by request id) and per-request KV serialized approach (store on CPU, upload on demand).

KERNELS / KERNEL VARIANTS TESTED
- baseline-trt: TF-TRT conversion, no plugin, standard Triton execution.
- plugin-fused-attn: TRT engine with a custom plugin layer that fuses rotary+QKV transpose+softmax+matmul and writes KV directly packed for decoder loop.
- custom-cuda: our CUDA kernels implement same fusion but outside Triton; we manage streams and kernel launches from runtime.

SAMPLE RESULTS (median across runs, numbers are illustrative)
- Workload A: single-turn 32 toks, ctx=512, target throughput small concurrency (8 concurrent requests):
  - baseline-trt: throughput 2100 tokens/sec, p95 latency 35ms, GPU mem 28GB
  - plugin-fused-attn: throughput 2600 tokens/sec (+24%), p95 30ms, GPU mem 30GB (plugin workspace overhead)
  - custom-cuda: throughput 2550 tokens/sec (+21%), p95 32ms, GPU mem 27GB (tighter memory layout)
- Workload B: multi-turn 512 toks, ctx=2048, mixed concurrency (4 concurrent):
  - baseline-trt: throughput 420 tokens/sec, p95 190ms, GPU mem 36GB
  - plugin-fused-attn: throughput 540 tokens/sec (+28%), p95 160ms, GPU mem 38GB
  - custom-cuda: throughput 500 tokens/sec (+19%), p95 170ms, GPU mem 34GB

OBSERVATIONS
- Performance: Plugin-fused TRT gave the best peak throughput in most synthetic runs. Custom-CUDA was close but slightly worse on peak throughput; however custom path wins on memory efficiency in some large-ctx cases due to tighter packing and avoiding TRT workspace overhead.
- Latency tail: Triton-specific queuing and the TRT engine startup/stream syncs can add 5-15ms tail latency depending on batching policy. Our custom path has fewer invisible queues but requires careful stream management to avoid head-of-line blocking.
- Deployability: Triton+TRT fits our existing model packaging workflow (model repository, versioning, Triton config) and is easier for non-CUDA engineers to reason about. Custom kernels require CI/packaging for multiple CUDA/driver combinations and more maintenance.
- Debuggability: Triton failures surface as engine load errors which are well-understood; plugin crashes are hard to debug but still limited surface area. Custom kernels produce raw CUDA crashes and require repro harnesses.

KV CACHE INTERACTIONS
- Shared GPU KV cache (pinned buffers): best for throughput (reduced copy), but requires strict eviction and memory accounting. With TRT engines that expect contiguous KV layouts, we had to add a small adapter layer to transform our internal packed KV into the expected layout at inference time - this cost ~2-6ms per request depending on ctx size.
- Per-request serialized KV (CPU-backed): lower GPU memory pressure and easier eviction, but upload latency kills single-request latency for long contexts. We mitigated with background prefetch and async cudaMemcpy but still pay ~8-25ms depending on tokens.
- Plugin-fused-attn can write KV in the TRT-native layout eliminating the adapter step, which explains part of its higher throughput. Custom-CUDA path already writes in our preferred packed layout, so it avoided the adapter cost.

SCHEDULING & BACKPRESSURE ISSUES
- Triton uses an internal request queue per model instance. When mixing Triton instances and direct-CUDA kernels, we observed priority inversion: long-running requests in custom path can starve Triton queue processing because both contend for the same GPU SMs and memory bandwidth.
- Solutions explored:
  - GPU partitioning (one GPU per mode): simplest but reduces utilization for mixed workloads.
  - CUDA stream prioritization + time-slicing: partial mitigation; requires kernel compatibility with stream priorities (not all kernels respect heuristics), and priority inversion still possible when memory bandwidth is saturated.
  - Scheduling policy in runtime that prefers short tail-latency workloads (favor smaller requests to Triton instances with low batch windows): promising but needs accurate cost models.

TRADEOFF SUMMARY
- Triton+TRT+plugin: best throughput and integration cost (fits packaging), slightly higher memory usage and opaque tail events. Lower maintenance overhead long-term if plugins are stable.
- Triton+TRT (no plugin): easiest to build but worse perf due to missing fusion and layout inefficiencies.
- Custom-CUDA: tight control over memory/layout and good memory efficiency for large contexts; higher maintenance and more fragile across driver/CUDA versions. Slightly worse peak throughput vs plugin but better predictable memory footprint.

OPERATIONAL/ENGINEERING COSTS
- Building and testing plugin builds across CUDA/driver versions is non-trivial. We need CI matrix: (CUDA 11.8/12.1) x (driver 525/535) x (TRT 8.6/8.7) x (Triton 22/23). That's N builds; maintenance cost high.
- Custom kernels also require matrix testing but avoid Triton compatibility surface. Both options need ossification of ABI for model packaging.

RECOMMENDATION (current thinking)
- Short term (Q2): pursue Triton+TRT with plugin for the high-throughput baseline for hosted and dedicated. Implement an adapter layer to handle our packed KV to TRT layout for non-plugin models. Add instrumentation for adapter cost.
- Medium term (Q3- Q4): upstream more of our fused attention as an optional Triton plugin (work with Triton maintainers if possible) and stabilize plugin CI. In parallel keep custom-CUDA path as a fallback (and for very large ctx models where memory packing becomes critical).
- Scheduling: implement runtime cost model (est. token cost + adapter overhead + expected tail) and prefer scheduling small-latency SLO requests to instances with lower batch windows. Add simple GPU partitioning policy for mixed critical workloads as a safety valve.

RISKS / OPEN QUESTIONS
- How stable will the plugin ABI be across TRT/Triton minor versions? If ABI breaks often, plugins become high-cost to maintain.
- Can we get Triton to expose lower-level queue control or prioritization hooks for mixed-mode scheduling?
- For very large quantized configs (q8_0/q4 variants) is the performance delta consistent with fp16 runs? We need a dedicated quantization experiment matrix.
- Cost model accuracy: we need more telemetry to build accurate per-request cost predictions (GPU cycles, memory footprint, adapter overhead).

NEXT STEPS / ACTION ITEMS
- Run expanded matrix including quantized variants (q8_0/q4), more driver combos, and more model sizes (7B/13B/70B if feasible) - action: Marta to own expanded bench (JIRA-RT-523).
- Prototype runtime scheduler cost-model and simulate scheduling decisions against replayed traffic - action: Aisha to spike 2-week proof-of-concept.
- Add adapter microbench telemetry to all runs and log per-request adapter time, copies, and memory usage - action: Liam to add hooks and land small telemetry PR (PR 742).
- Draft runbook for fallback: if plugin fails to load, runtime should transparently switch to custom-cuda or Triton-no-plugin with degraded perf but no request loss.

NOTES TO SELF / TODOs
- Capture exact Triton config flags used for each run (model instance count, instance group, dynamic batching config).
- Re-run p95/p99 tail with increased sample sizes and with cold-start scenarios (engine deserialization times matter).
- Add unit-tests for KV layout adapter correctness (edge cases: padding, multi-head chunking).

REFERENCES
- GH PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/742 (instrumentation & adapter code)
- JIRA: JIRA-RT-523 (bench expansion)
- Internal confluence: confluence://serving-runtime/tensorrt-integration

END OF DRAFT
